title: Entropy-driven phase-splitting and fairness policy for prefill/decode
creator: Maya Thompson
description: Problem: Current prefill/decode scheduler uses static phase split heuristics that trade latency and throughput poorly for variable input complexity. High-entropy prompts (open-ended generation) and requests with sparse attention patterns cause long tail latency and increased per-token cost. Goal: design and implement an entropy-driven phase-splitting policy that adapts phase boundaries and microbatching based on per-request entropy and attention sparsity signals, while enforcing tenant-aware fairness credits to prevent noisy tenants from monopolizing low-latency fast-paths.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New scheduler can adapt phase splits per-request using entropy and attention-sparsity features; 2) P99 decode latency for latency-tier requests decreases by >=8% on aggregate without dropping throughput by >5%; 3) No tenant sees >15% regression in median latency compared to baseline; 4) Can be toggled with runtime config and rolled back if regressions detected.
implementation_plan: 1) Add entropy estimator hook in request preprocessor (lightweight byte-level and model-token entropy approximation). 2) Surface attention-sparsity hint from kernel-level profiler to scheduler. 3) Implement PhaseSplitter module: ruleset that uses entropy+attention to choose split points and microbatch size; integrates tenant credit windows. 4) Implement simulator to model fairness/throughput tradeoffs. 5) Run offline sims, then staged canary on dedicated capacity, then gradual rollout to hosted. 6) Add observability: per-request entropy, chosen split, kernel selection, downstream latency buckets.
design_notes: - Use an approximate entropy metric (Shannon estimate over token distribution of first N tokens) to avoid heavy compute on hot path. - Attention-sparsity inferred from average attention head activations and kernel probe hints; avoids full attention matrix compute. - Tenant credits: sliding window of consumed low-latency tokens; credits decay exponentially. - Fallback: if kernel probe suggests incompatible kernel (quantized fastpath not available), fallback to default two-phase split to avoid functional changes.
tradeoffs: - Aggressive entropy-based splitting improves p99 for complex prompts but may slightly reduce batching efficiency for short prompts. - Adding entropy hooks increases prefill CPU overhead (~0.5-1%); acceptable vs latency gain. - Tenant credits prevent starvation but add scheduler bookkeeping and state; needs efficient sharding by GPU node.
metrics_and_observability: Primary: p50/p95/p99 latency for latency-tier and throughput-tier; tokens/sec; cost-per-1M-tokens. Secondary: kernel selection distribution, microbatch utilization, tenant credit balance, rollback triggers. Dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd/prefill-decode-experiments. Simulation results stored in S3: s3://redwood-inference-experiments/entropy-scheduler/2026-02.
experiment_plan: Phase A: Offline simulation (1 week) across workload traces (chatbot, summarization, code). Phase B: Canary on 5% of latency-tier traffic on dedicated pool (2 weeks). Phase C: A/B test 20% vs baseline for mixed traffic (3 weeks). Phase D: Gradual ramp to 100% with rollback guardrails (alerts on >10% p99 regressions).
implementation_todo: - PR: runtime change (scheduler + preproc) https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7890 - Confluence spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Entropy+Driven+Scheduler - Simulation harness PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/tools/pull/334 - Add Grafana panels and alerts (team infra).
risks: 1) Entropy estimator misclassifies prompts causing worse batching -> mitigate by conservative thresholds and feature flag. 2) Kernel hints may be noisy across different GPUs leading to split oscillation -> add hysteresis and minimum phase duration. 3) Tenant-credit state blowup on large clusters -> use approximate counters with bounded memory.
notes: Initial prototype built in spike branch spike/entropy-split (internal). Early microbenchmarks show 9-12% p99 reduction for long-form generation on A100 80GB with attention-sparsity hints. Cost impact estimated -2% tokens/sec for short prompts but net cost/per-response decreases for complex workloads.
